The pitch document, lightly cleaned up. Cats. Friends. Mild incompetence. ## The pitch Four friends. A cafe. Thirty cats. The health inspector comes on Tuesday. That was the original pitch document. It fit in a text message. The version I sent to my friends was: "chaotic co-op kitchen game but with cats instead of customers and the cats are also the problem." ## Why co-op Because the best gaming memories I have are shared ones. Because Overcooked exists and people love it. Because I wanted to make something my friends would actually play. ## Why cats Cats are chaos engines with legible motivations. You always know *why* the cat knocked the cup off the counter. (Spite. It was spite.) That legibility makes them funny rather than frustrating — and funny chaos is the core tone I'm after. ## What this is actually about A game about helping each other with a problem that keeps getting worse. The cats aren't the antagonists. The cats are the condition you're operating under.
FOOTNOTE · 001.A "The best co-op games are about the relationship between the players, not the obstacles they're facing."
Three months in — what the game is now
A short year-end checkpoint. Things I expected. Things I didn't.

A short year-end checkpoint. Things I expected. Things I didn't. ## What I expected That building a co-op game would be harder than a single-player game. (Correct.) That cat AI would be a solved problem I could implement quickly. (Incorrect.) ## What I didn't expect That the kitchen layout would matter this much. The spacing between stations determines whether co-op feels like teamwork or chaos. Too close: players collide constantly. Too far: they might as well be playing alone. We've rebuilt the floor plan four times. Also: that people would get attached to specific cats after ten minutes with a prototype. Biscuit already has fans. ## Where we are Core loop works. Networking is held together with optimism and latency compensation. The cats have personalities. The coffee spills correctly. This is a real game now, not just a jam project that kept going.
FOOTNOTE · 002.A "A game is real when players argue about the best strategy. We're there."
Switching the prototype from Godot to Unity
I love Godot. I also needed multiplayer to just work. The unsentimental version of that decision.

I love Godot. I also needed multiplayer to just work. The unsentimental version of that decision. ## Why Godot first I started in Godot 4 because I know it well and the iteration speed is excellent for prototyping. The first two months of Catastrophe Cafe were built there: basic cat movement, a simple kitchen layout, the core interaction model. ## Why we switched Multiplayer. Godot's high-level networking is good, but it requires more manual work than I had bandwidth for while also designing the game. Unity's Netcode for GameObjects — imperfect as it is — has more solved problems and more documentation for the specific patterns I needed (object ownership, state synchronization, latency compensation). The switch took two weeks. Most systems ported cleanly. The cat personalities required a full rewrite because of how Godot's signals differ from Unity's event system. ## What I miss Gdscript. Just being honest.
FOOTNOTE · 003.A "The right tool is the one that lets you finish the thing. Sentiment is for after you ship."
Latte art with a particle system
You can make a passable rosetta with eight particles and a curve. Here is the curve.

You can make a passable rosetta with eight particles and a curve. Here is the curve. ## The approach Latte art is a minigame. You have a limited window — the pour — to trace a pattern. We represent the pour as a stream of particles that fall into the cup and interact with a surface-tension simulation (very simple: particles push each other laterally and settle toward the center). A rosetta pattern requires eight particles placed along a bezier curve, with specific timing between each. The result isn't photorealistic, but it reads as latte art to anyone who's ever made one. ## Why it works The secret is the pour angle. Tilting the cup slightly (represented in-game by a held button) changes the flow direction. Players learn this intuitively because it mirrors real espresso technique. The mechanic teaches itself.
FOOTNOTE · 004.A "Eight particles and a curve. That's it. That's the whole thing."
Designing cats as small state machines. Plus, why one of them refuses to drink from a bowl.

Designing cats as small state machines. Plus, why one of them refuses to drink from a bowl. ## The architecture Each cat is a small state machine with four base states: Wandering, Curious, Demanding, and Napping. State transitions are driven by a combination of environment (loud noise? fire?) and personality weights. Personality is three floats: curiosity, grumpiness, and hunger urgency. These don't change what the states *do* — they change how quickly the cat moves between them and how it behaves within each state. ## The cat that won't drink from bowls Cat #17 — internally called "Biscuit" — has a curiosity weight of 0.9 and a grumpiness weight of 0.8. In testing, these values interacted in a way we didn't anticipate: Biscuit would approach a water bowl, sniff it (Curious), decide it was unacceptable (Grumpy), and walk away. Every time. We kept it. Some bugs are features.
FOOTNOTE · 005.A "A cat with opinions is more interesting than a cat without them, even if the opinion is 'no.'"
On chaos that is not punishing
Playtests said the kitchen felt mean. The mechanics didn't change. The feedback did. A field report on game-feel.

Playtests said the kitchen felt mean. The mechanics didn't change. The feedback did. A field report on game-feel. ## What happened Three separate playtest sessions ended with the same note: "the kitchen feels mean." The players weren't failing more than we expected. They were failing at the same rate. But something in how the failure was communicated made it feel unfair rather than fun. ## The diagnosis We were telling players *what went wrong* before they had a chance to feel bad about it. The cat knocked over the coffee: error sound, red flash, score penalty — all at the same instant. There was no moment of "oh no" before the consequence. In a game where chaos is the point, chaos should feel like comedy, not punishment. The fix was simple: add a beat. Let the cup wobble before it falls. Let the player see it coming and *almost* catch it. ## What changed Nothing mechanical. The same things happen at the same rates. But each failure now has a wind-up. Players laugh instead of groaning. The kitchen still burns down — but now it burns down entertainingly.
FOOTNOTE · 006.A "The difference between funny chaos and frustrating chaos is one beat of anticipation."
When two players grab the same bowl across 80ms of latency, who wins? A short note on authoritative kitchens.

When two players grab the same bowl across 80ms of latency, who wins? A short note on authoritative kitchens. ## The problem Two players reach for the same bowl of soup at the same time. On each client, they each see themselves holding it. On the server, only one of them can be right. This is the fundamental problem of multiplayer object ownership. ## The solution The server is always authoritative about who holds what. When a player tries to pick something up, they send a request. The server grants it or denies it. On the client, we *predict* the pickup immediately (optimistic update), then reconcile when the server responds. If the server says "no, the other player got it first," we snap back. This produces a brief visual glitch — but 80ms of latency means it's nearly invisible in practice. The harder problem is visual continuity. We lerp the bowl back to its correct position rather than teleporting it. Players notice the correction less when it's smooth.
FOOTNOTE · 007.A "Authoritative servers don't prevent disagreements. They just decide them faster than the players notice."
Three rewrites in, the cats finally walk around the espresso machine instead of through it. Here's the navmesh trick I should have used in March.

Three rewrites in, the cats finally walk around the espresso machine instead of through it. Here's the navmesh trick I should have used in March. ## What I tried The first three approaches all had the same flaw: I was treating the cats like player characters and giving them a full navigation agent. Cats don't navigate. Cats *wander with intention*. The espresso machine wasn't an obstacle to route around — it was a surface to consider jumping onto. The fix was splitting movement into two systems: a coarse pathfinding layer (A* on a baked navmesh) and a local steering layer (simple avoidance radius). The coarse layer finds a general path. The local layer handles the last half-meter of "I can't quite fit through here." ## What worked Baking the navmesh with a smaller agent radius than the cat's visual size. The cats look bigger than they navigate. This gives them a slightly floating quality — which, honestly, is accurate to real cats.
FOOTNOTE · 008.A "The fourth rewrite is the one that works because you finally understand what you were doing in the first three."
What I learned scoping, cutting, and finishing Agneepath in a day. The honest version.

What I learned scoping, cutting, and finishing Agneepath in a day. The honest version. ## The constraint I gave myself 24 hours to build and ship a complete game. No cheating on scope ("I'll just finish this one thing after the timer"). Whatever was in at hour 23 was what shipped. The result was Agneepath — a 2D action platformer with one level, one boss, and hand-tuned physics. It shipped. I'm still surprised. ## What the constraint does to your brain The first six hours I wasted on architecture. I was building a game framework instead of a game. The constraint eventually forced me to stop — not by wisdom, but by running out of time. Hours seven through twelve were the real work. With no time for abstraction, I wrote the simplest code that could possibly work. Functions that do one thing. Variables with obvious names. No generalization. It was the cleanest code I'd written in months. ## What got cut - A second level (obvious) - A dash ability (almost done — cut at hour 18) - Music (made a sound effect loop work harder) - The story (one line of text in the title screen: "go forward") Every cut made the game better. The dash would have required rebalancing the boss. The second level would have been rushed. The music placeholder I had was wrong for the tone. ## The honest lesson You know what you need earlier than you're willing to admit. The cuts I made at hour 18 were obvious at hour 6. The game that shipped was the game I should have scoped at the start. The 24-hour constraint didn't teach me to work faster. It taught me to decide faster.
FOOTNOTE · N-01 "The scope you're willing to cut is the game you should have made from the start."
On the texture of mission paper
Why every interface I love has the same faint warmth — and what dark UIs miss when they reach for pure white.

Why every interface I love has the same faint warmth — and what dark UIs miss when they reach for pure white. ## The observation I've been collecting screenshots of interfaces for about two years. Dark UIs, mostly — games, terminals, specialized software. The ones I keep coming back to have something in common that took me a while to name. None of them use pure white text. They use cream. Warm off-whites. Colors that feel like they have a history — like the text was printed on something that had already been used. ## Why it works Pure white on a dark background creates maximum contrast, which sounds correct until you sit with it for an hour and notice that your eyes are tired. The contrast is too stark. There's no warmth in the relationship between the foreground and background. Warm cream text on a near-black background gives you readable contrast without the harshness. The warmth creates a sense of material — like you're reading something real rather than looking at a light source. ## What dark UIs get wrong Most dark UIs reach for dark gray backgrounds and light gray text and stop there. The result is readable but characterless. It's the UI equivalent of wearing all beige. The interfaces I love pick a temperature and commit to it. Cold dark backgrounds with cool blue-white text. Warm dark backgrounds with cream text. The key is that the foreground and background are in the same color family — related, not just contrasted. ## The mission paper principle Old documents have warmth because they're made of something. Paper yellows. Ink fades. The imperfection is the character. Digital interfaces can borrow this. Not by adding grain or texture (though that helps), but by choosing colors that feel aged — like they've been somewhere, done something.
FOOTNOTE · N-02 "The best dark interfaces feel like they were printed on the back of something important."
